title: High elongation of medium-manganese steel containing 1.0 wt.% Al after a short intercritical annealing time
abstract: This paper presents research on the phase transformation, microstructure, and tensile properties of medium-manganese steel containing 1.0 wt.% Al (1.0Al) after a short intercritical annealing (IA) time at different IA temperatures using thermodynamic simulation, scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffractometry, and uniaxial tensile tests. The results show that the addition of 1.0Al can expand the size of the IA temperature range from 208 to 272 °C and shifts the range to higher temperatures, and this increases the fractions of the retained austenite in the steel when the IA time is short. Most of the retained austenite transforms to α’-martensite during the tensile test. Part of the retained austenite transforms to α’-martensite in the early stage and contributes little plasticity. The other part of the retained austenite transforms in the middle or late tensile deformation stage and improves the mechanical properties. The mechanical properties of the steel are remarkable, with a tensile strength above 1000 MPa, elongation above 35%, and strength × ductility above 35,000 MPa% when the IA temperature is 700 °C and the IA time is 3 min.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In the last several decades, advanced high-strength steels (AHSS)—such as, dual-phase (DP) steel, transformation-induced plasicity (TRIP) steel, and quenching and partitioning (QP) steel—have been used with great success in the automobile industry  [1–5] . These steels are used in the structural parts of the “body-in-white” to improve fuel efficiency and safety as well as to reduce CO 2  emissions. AHSS have been developed from their first to third-generation  [6–8] . In recent years, third-generation AHSS under development have been designed to achieve a balance between acceptable cost and remarkable mechanical properties.

Among the various types of third-generation AHSS, medium-manganese steels are considered a strong candidate  [9–11] . The fine microstructures of medium-manganese steels are composed mainly of retained austenite and ferrite/martensite, and show an excellent balance of high strength and high elongation. This type of microstructure is obtained via an intercritical annealing (IA) process at a temperature between the start (A 1 ) and finish (A 3 ) temperatures of the austenite reverse transformation from ferrite (α) or from α’-martensite after rolling  [11–15] .

The IA process is critical because it determines the constituted phases that further govern the mechanical properties. Specifically, the fraction and the stability of austenite are critical to elongation via the TRIP effect. They are associated with an enhanced elongation due to the formation of martensite during deformation, which increases the work-hardening rate and thus delays necking  [16,17] . The stability of the retained austenite is affected by many factors, including composition, grain size, morphology, and the distribution of retained austenite; the composition of the retained austenite is the most relevant factor  [18–21] . Carbon and manganese are the most important stability elements for retained austenite in medium-manganese steels. During IA, carbon and manganese partition from α or α’-martensite to austenite, and a longer IA time is often required because of the slow diffusion of manganese  [22] . In today’s modern steel industry, a continuous annealing production line is widely applied due to its high efficiency. However, when using this type of production line, the IA time is shortened to only a few minutes. Therefore, it is important to study and improve the mechanical performance within such a short IA time. Increasing the IA temperature is the easiest way to solve the problems that result from a short IA duration, but this method is unavailable for medium-manganese TRIP steels in which the IA temperature range is narrow, because the increased IA temperature will decrease the stability of the reverse austenite  [9,23] .

If the IA temperature range can be expanded and shifted to higher temperatures when the IA temperature is increased within a suitable range, the stability of the reverse austenite will not be decreased, and the increased IA temperature approach can be used. The addition of aluminum (Al) can significantly raise the A 3  temperature and slightly influence the A 1  temperature  [24] . Therefore, Al has the effect of expanding the IA temperature and increasing its range. It is worth noting that Al is useful and that some steel with a high Al content has excellent mechanical properties due to the special function of delta-ferrite  [25,26] . But, the addition of Al introduces some problems, such as alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) inclusion and a decreased rate of continuous casting  [27] . Therefore, the content of Al should be limited to a suitable range.

Research works have shown that the addition of Al in traditional hot-dip galvanizing TRIP steels as an alloying element has partially or completely replaced Si, and that the content of Al is between 1.0 and 1.5 wt.%  [3,28,29] . Based on the previous research, 1.0 wt.% Al (1.0Al) was added to medium-manganese steel in this study. We studied the influence of Al on the critical transformation temperature point in the IA temperature range and investigated the effect of the IA process on the microstructure and mechanical properties of 0.2C–5 Mn (wt.%) steel compared to the mechanical properties and the IA process with an alloy in the absence of Al.

sections.heading: Material and Methods
paragraphs:
Fe–0.20C–5.00Mn – 1.00Al–0.50Si (wt.%) was selected as the nominal composition and was used in CALPHAD calculation. The composition of cast ingot prepared by vacuum induction melting is Fe–0.19C–5.35 Mn – 0.95Al–0.51Si (wt.%). The ingot was solution-treated at 1200 °C for 60 min, hot-rolled at approximately 950 °C into 3.5 mm thick plates, maintained at 600 °C for 1.5 h, and subsequently furnace-cooled to room temperature for the coiling simulation. The hot-rolled plates were pickled in a 25 vol. % HCl solution and subsequently cold-rolled to 1.4-mm-thick sheets (60% reduction) at room temperature. The transformation temperatures of A 1  and A 3  were calculated as 555 and 806 °C, respectively, using Factsage® 7.1 software and FSstel databases. Thus, five temperatures (640, 670, 700, 730, and 760 °C) were chosen for IA. Specimens (25 × 100 mm) were then cut from the cold-rolled plate and intercritically annealed in a salt bath for 3 min for further microstructure characterization and mechanical testing. The above-mentioned heat treatment is schematically illustrated in  Fig. 1 
                      .

The microstructures of the specimens were investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ZEISS-Gemini 300) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL F200) operated at 200 kV. The sample for SEM was mechanically ground and subsequently electrolyzed with a solution with 85 vol. % CH 3 COOH and 15 vol. % HClO 4 . Thin foil specimens for TEM were mechanically ground to a thickness of 50 μm and punched to round disks (ø 3 mm), followed by electropolishing at −20 °C in a twin-jet polisher using a solution of 95 vol. % CH 3 COOH and 5 vol. % HClO 4 .

The volume fractions of the retained austenite were measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D8 ADVANCE) with a Cu target. Specimens for the XRD were prepared first by mechanical polishing, and then by electropolishing at 15 V at room temperature in a solution of 20 vol. % HClO 4  and 80 vol. % CH 3 COOH. Tensile specimens from the heat-treated samples were prepared with a dog-bone shape and a gauge length and width of 25 and 6.5 mm along the rolling direction, respectively. Tensile tests were carried out at room temperature in a CMT universal testing machine with a load range of 300 K N. The cross-head speed was maintained at 2 mm min –1  (strain rate of 6.67 × 10 –4  s –1 ). Two specimens were tested for each heat treatment.

sections.heading: Influence of Al on the equilibrium phase fractions
paragraphs:
Using the CALPHAD method  [31] , the phase fractions in the steels with 1.0Al added and without Al after IA at different temperatures were calculated; the results are shown in  Fig. 2 
                         (a) and (b). The ferrite, retained austenite, cementite, and martensite phases are denoted as F, RA, C, and M, respectively. Four critical temperatures, which describe the expected phase transformation behavior, are shown in  Fig. 2  by vertical lines: the start temperature of austenite formation (A 1 ), finish temperature of austenite formation (A 3 ), cementite dissolution temperature (A CM ), and an IA temperature where the Ms of the reverse austenite equals room temperature (M 0 )  [32] . At temperatures above A 3 , fully austenitic microstructures (reverse austenite) exist at the IA temperature and most of the reverse austenite transforms to fresh martensite during the final cooling stage. Ferrite and cementite are present below the temperatures of A 3  and A CM , respectively. The reverse austenite is fully stabilized by solute partitioning at IA temperatures below M 0 , and no fresh martensite is present below M 0 .

The addition of Al can increase the four critical temperatures; the A 3  temperature shows the most significant increase from 719 °C for the steel without Al to 788 °C for the steel with 1.0Al added. With 1.0Al additions, the IA temperature range between A 1  and A 3  is widened from 208 to 272 °C and the range shifts to higher temperatures. The difference between the M 0  and A CM  temperatures changes from 31 to −3 °C with the addition of 1.0Al. The predicted volume fraction of retained austenite (f RA ) peak shifts to higher temperature and greater value. The maximum predicted f RA  values for the steel without Al and with the addition of 1.0Al are obtained at the A CM  temperature, with values of 27.8 and 30.8%, respectively.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                          illustrates the microstructures of the investigated samples.  Fig. 3 (a), (c), (e), (g), and (i) are the microstructure of the sample after IA and before tensile testing.

The figures show that the microstructure annealed at different temperatures contains a certain amount of ferrite (F) and a part of the retained austenite (RA). When the IA temperature is 640 or 670 °C, there is no obvious phase transformation in the microstructure, only incomplete recrystallization of ferrite. White grains appear in the samples annealed at relatively low temperatures (640 –700 °C), which are presumed to be cementite (C); the content of cementite decreases when the IA temperature increased. The sample annealed at 730 °C includes an additional phase, which is thought to be fresh martensite (M f ) transformed from the reversed austenite upon cooling. The main reason for this phenomenon is that as the temperature increases, the reversed austenite grains grow, and the carbon and manganese in the reversed austenite are insufficient to maintain the reversed austenite’s stability. As such, martensitic transformation occurs in the subsequent cooling process, so the fresh martensite begins to appear and gradually increases  [15,23] .

Fig. 3 (b), (d), (f), (h), and (j) show the microstructure of interrupted tensile test specimens. Compared with  Fig. 3  (a), (c), (e), (g), and (i), the microstructures of the samples indicate that no obvious phase transformation occurs at relatively low temperatures (640 and 670 °C) after the tensile test. This is due to the high stability of the retained austenite at this temperature and the difficulty of a phase transformation occurring during the tensile test. It is speculated that the material has a low total elongation at this temperature. A large amount of retained austenite is transformed into α’-martensite (M RA ) at 700 and 730 °C. The retained austenite in the microstructure of the interrupted tensile test specimens is mostly granular austenite, because the stability of granular austenite is better than that of block retained austenite. In addition, the microstructure deforms greatly along the tensile direction, with the deformation most obvious at 700 °C. Therefore, it can be speculated that the best mechanical properties can be obtained by annealing at this temperature. Similar to the microstructure before the tensile test, the microstructure of the interrupted tensile test specimens at 760 °C is mainly martensite. Therefore, it can be speculated that the specimen has a higher tensile strength at this temperature.

TEM was used to study the austenite deformation in more detail. The interrupted tensile test specimens were investigated, and the results for the 700 °C sample are shown in  Fig. 4 
                          and  Fig. 5 
                         . For this specimen, strain/stress-induced α’-martensite is formed from the austenite during the tensile straining. It can be found that most of the retained austenite is transformed to α’-martensite during the tensile deformation. It is observed that martensite is either polygonal or elongated, corresponding to retained austenite with a lower stability transformed at a small strain and retained austenite with a higher stability transformed at a higher strain, respectively.

One example of the polygonal shape is shown in  Fig. 4 . The grain is not severely deformed, indicating that the prior-austenite was not very stable and transformed to martensite at the early stage of deformation. Therefore, this austenite transformation in the early stage contributed little to plasticity. One example of the elongated shape is shown in  Fig. 5 . It formed from one retained austenite grain (marked with a red circle) that transformed in the middle or late tensile deformation stage. This austenite-martensite transformation during the tensile deformation can improve plasticity, which is well known as the TRIP effect  [33] . Further observation shows that most of the austenite first deformed greatly and later transformed to martensite. The transformation may result in different variants of martensite. In  Fig. 5 (a), areas B and D are both fully martensitic, while the crystal orientations of them ( Figs. 5 (b) and 5(d)) are different. This transformation could also be incomplete, as area C in  Fig. 5 (a) contains martensite and retained austenite ( Fig. 5 (c)). The diffraction of retained austenite can be observed both in  Fig. 4 (b) and  Fig. 5 (c), which means that untransformed retained austenite exists near both of the two different shapes of α’-martensite.

Fig. 6 
                         (a) shows the XRD patterns of the specimens subjected to IA treatment at different temperatures. The volume fractions of the retained austenite are calculated according to eq.  (1)  and are shown in  Fig. 6 (b). This figure shows that with an increase in the IA temperature, the retained austenite of the 1.0Al alloy annealed at different temperatures initially increases, exhibits a maximum at temperatures near 700 °C, and dramatically decreases at higher temperatures. The maximum retained austenite value is 26.64%, which is higher than the calculated value shown in  Fig. 2 (b), and is presumed to be related to the diffusion of the elements and the size of the grains in the critical annealing process. The results from XRD are comparable with the aforementioned microstructure observations; in the microstructure of the samples, no obvious phase transformation occurs at relatively low temperatures (640 and 670 °C) after the tensile test. Part of the retained austenite transforms into martensite during the tensile test at relatively high temperatures (700 – 760 °C), and the content of retained austenite decreases. At 700 °C, the retained austenite is only 6.15% after the tensile test. About 77% of the retained austenite transforms into α’-martensite due to the strain/stress during the tensile straining. Therefore, it can be speculated that the best mechanical properties are obtained at this temperature.

The microstructure observations from the micrographs and XRD can be summarized as follows. When the IA temperature is increased above 640 °C, the f RA  increases. When the IA temperature is increased above 700 °C, the reverse austenite partly transforms to fresh martensite, leading to a decrease in the retained austenite. The tendency for the reverse austenite to transform into fresh martensite upon final cooling increases by increasing the IA temperature. Retained austenite transforms into α’-martensite due to either strain or stress during tensile straining, and the f RA  values are dramatically reduced.

sections.heading: General mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The yield strength (YS), tensile strength (TS), total elongation (TEL), and tensile strength × total elongation (TS × TEL) of the investigated steels with added 1.0Al annealed at different IA temperatures are summarized in  Table 1 
                            .

To compare with values in the literature  [12,34–38] , the mechanical properties of steels from previous research, without Al and after different IA processes, are plotted in  Fig. 7 
                            , and a simple comparison is made with the investigated steel. In comparison with the literature data, the investigated steel with added 1.0Al after different IA processes shows better TS and TEL in a shorter IA time period. The addition of Al gives the medium-manganese steel superior mechanical properties after a short annealing time. In particular, the TS × TEL value of the investigated steel reaches about 39 GPa% at 700 °C, which meets the target of 30 GPa% for third-generation AHHS used in the automotive industry  [12,13] .

sections.heading: Influence of IA temperature on the mechanical properties
paragraphs:
Fig. 8 
                             shows the measured room-temperature tensile flow curves for the investigated steel annealed at an IA temperature ranging from 640 to 760 °C followed by air cooling. The tensile deformation characteristics are strongly influenced by the IA temperature. For example, the total elongation when annealed at 640 °C is 6.08%, and the value greatly increases up to 36.36% for the sample annealed at 700 °C. In addition, the maximum TS value of 1591.2 MPa obtained at 760 °C is 1.5 times as large as the minimum value of 1047.9 MPa obtained at 670 °C. As expected, samples annealed at 700 °C have higher f RA  values and exhibit relatively larger elongations. A greater TS is observed in the samples annealed above 730 °C, which have higher martensite fractions. The tensile curves from the samples annealed at 730 and 760 °C show high tensile strength and small elongations. These results are similar to the typical curves of fresh martensite, because the initial microstructure before the tensile test contains a large amount of fresh martensite.

The variations in the mechanical properties with annealing temperature are shown in  Fig. 9 
                            . As the temperature increases, YS decreases monotonously while the TS first decreases until 670 °C and then increases by more than 500 MPa from 670 to 760 °C (see  Table 1 ).

Based on the previous microstructure observations, when the IA temperature is 640–670 °C, there is no obvious phase transformation in the structure; only the recovery and/or incomplete recrystallization of ferrite and the dissolution of cementite occur. The decrease of tensile strength from 640 to 670 °C is due to the recovery and incomplete recrystallization of ferrite. When the annealing temperature is 700 °C, the reverse austenite has a high stability, and can be fully retained at room temperature; thus, the TRIP effect occurs during the tensile process, and increases TS. At 730 and 760 °C, part of the reverse austenite transforms into martensite after IA due to the low stability of the reverse austenite, which is the main reason for the rapid increase of the TS. The YS decreases monotonously with an increase in the IA temperature. This result suggests that the YS is related to the degree of grain recovery and/or recrystallization, and the retained austenite and martensite contents. With an increase in the IA temperature, the grain grows and the dislocation density decreases, which is also beneficial to dislocation slip and YS decrease. The TEL appears to reach a maximum at 700 °C and then decreases as the temperature increases. This result is attributed to the largest fraction of retained austenite after IA being found at 700 °C, which can induce the most significant TRIP effect during the tensile deformation. However, the fraction of retained austenite does not have a large effect on the YS of the material because there are few martensitic transformations in the early stages of plastic deformation during the tensile test  [31] .

The TRIP effect persists during the deformation process because the stability of the retained austenite varies. The block retained austenite has low stability, and it is easy to produce the TRIP effect at the initial stage of deformation, while the granular retained austenite has good stability and can produce the TRIP effect in the middle and late stages of deformation  [39,40] . Therefore, the strain hardening behavior of the steels is altered depending on the IA temperature because the IA temperature determines the stability of the retained austenite and the work hardening behavior with different IA processes (see  Fig. 10 
                            ). The 700 and 730 °C samples show a three-stage strain hardening. The variation in the value of the true strain with deformation indicates that the TRIP effect persists during the deformation process, which is the main reason for the good elongation of the investigated steel.

When the true strain of the 700 °C sample reaches about 0.11, the true stress value begins to rise and increases slowly until fracture takes place. This is due to the high content and stability of retained austenite in the 700 °C sample; this retained austenite cannot be transformed by a low strain during deformation. With an increase in the strain, the retained austenite continuously transforms into martensite. The true stress value of the 730 °C sample increases rapidly when the true strain value reaches about 0.035, and then it decreases rapidly. This indicates that the stability of the retained austenite in the 730 °C sample is not as good as that of the retained austenite in the 700 °C sample, and that the TRIP effect occurs at a lower strain  [31,39] .

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This paper presents the results of research into the microstructure and tensile properties of medium-manganese steel with 1.0Al added, after IA at a temperature ranging from 640 to 760 °C for a short time (3 min). The following conclusions can be drawn. First, the addition of 1.0Al expands the size of the IA temperature range from 208 to 272 °C, and the range shifts to higher temperatures, which contributes to improving the fractions of retained austenite. The 700 °C sample has a high (25%) fraction of retained austenite. Second, martensite is either polygonal or elongated, corresponding to retained austenite with a lower stability transformed at a small strain and retained austenite with a higher stability transformed at a higher strain, respectively. The retained austenite transformed in the early stage contributes little to plasticity, while that transformed in the middle or late tensile deformation stage improves the mechanical properties. Third, the steel with added 1.0Al obtains excellent mechanical properties with a brief IA time. The best mechanical properties were obtained at 700 °C, the tensile strength was 1068 MPa, the elongation was 36.36%, and the strength × ductility was 38.83 GPa%.
